meta.title: Who really said "I can't write a book commensurate with Shakespeare, but I can write a book by me"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dale Carnegie quoted it in 1948. Oxford professor Walter Alexander Raleigh wrote it in a letter on 28 April 1907 — not the Elizabethan explorer.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I can't write a book commensurate with Shakespeare, but I can write a book by me'?
meta.ogDescription: Written by Oxford professor Walter Alexander Raleigh in a 1907 letter to T. H. Warren — not Dale Carnegie, and not Sir Walter Raleigh the explorer.

answer.label: Not Dale Carnegie — actually Walter Alexander Raleigh
answer.authorDates: 1861–1922 · Oxford’s first Professor of English Literature
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from a letter Walter Alexander Raleigh — the Oxford English professor, not the Elizabethan explorer — wrote to T. H. Warren, President of Magdalen College, on 28 April 1907, first printed in The Letters of Sir Walter Raleigh (1879–1922), Volume 2 ↗ (Methuen, 1926) at page 314. Dale Carnegie quoted it in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) and credited Professor Raleigh by name; as Quote Investigator documents ↗, Carnegie is the popularizer, not the author.

source.heading: The letter, 28 April 1907

source.excerpt: Everyone says it was a horribly difficult thing to write on Shakespeare. So it was and is, I suppose, but I didn’t think of it that way, or I couldn’t have written. I can’t write a book commensurate with Shakespeare, but I can write a book by me,—which is all that any one can do. I feel as free to think about Shakespeare as to think about the moon, without putting myself into competition. So I was not conscious of impudence, or even of ambition.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ is the anchor here, and its conclusion is unambiguous: Professor Walter Alexander Raleigh deserves credit for a statement he wrote in a letter in 1907, and it was not penned by Sir Walter Raleigh of the Elizabethan era. QI cites the letter to Thomas Herbert Warren, dated April 28, 1907, published in the 1926 Letters, volume 2, page 314.

We checked the primary source rather than taking it on trust: the OCR of the 1926 Methuen volume 2 ↗ carries the heading “To T. H. Warren, President of Magdalen” on page 314, followed by the sentence in exactly this wording — matching QI’s citation.

The author is the Oxford man, not the explorer: Wikipedia ↗ gives his dates as 5 September 1861 – 13 May 1922, records that he was the first holder of Oxford’s Chair of English Literature from 1904, and lists his Shakespeare (1907) — scanned in full at the Internet Archive ↗ — the book he is discussing in the letter.

Where the wrong credit comes from: Carnegie quoted the line in 1948 and named Professor Raleigh, but later compilations dropped the distinction, and aggregator pages ↗ now cite the 1926 Letters while labelling the author with the Elizabethan explorer’s dates.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1926 Methuen printing, volume 2, page 314. Note the clause that almost always gets dropped in circulation: “—which is all that any one can do.”

source.rightsNote: The wording is from a letter written in 1907 and first published in The Letters of Sir Walter Raleigh (1879–1922) (Methuen, London) in 1926 — before 1931, so the volume is in the public domain in the United States; Raleigh himself died in 1922. Dale Carnegie’s 1948 How to Stop Worrying and Start Living, where many readers first met the line, remains in copyright, which is why we quote Raleigh’s letter and only describe Carnegie’s use of it.

author.name: Walter Alexander Raleigh
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: About Walter Alexander Raleigh
author.metaLine: 1861–1922 · Oxford's first Professor of English Literature
author.bio: Sir Walter Alexander Raleigh (1861–1922) was the first holder of the Chair of English Literature at Oxford, a post he held from 1904 until his death, and a fellow of Merton College from 1914. He wrote Style (1897), Milton (1900) and the well-received Shakespeare (1907) — the book whose reception prompted this remark — and was working on an official history of the war in the air when he died. His correspondence was gathered after his death and published as The Letters of Sir Walter Raleigh (1879–1922) in 1926, edited by Lady Raleigh; he shares a name, and constant credit-confusion, with the Elizabethan statesman who died in 1618.

misattribution.heading: Two wrong names, one right one
misattribution.intro: This sentence circulates under two names that did not write it. One is a case of mistaken identity between two men called Sir Walter Raleigh; the other is the bestselling author who quoted it accurately and got the credit anyway.

items.who: Sir Walter Raleigh, the Elizabethan statesman and explorer (died 1618)
items.why: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is blunt: the quotation was not penned by the Sir Walter Raleigh of the Elizabethan era, and the ambiguous name is the whole problem. The credit spread through compilations that printed the bare name — QI documents Andrew McAleer’s 2008 The 101 Habits of Highly Successful Novelists repeating it ↗ — and today aggregators such as LibQuotes ↗ cite the correct 1926 Letters while attaching the explorer’s dates, 1552–1618, and a 2019 blog post reprints it as by “Sir Walter Raleigh (1554-1618), English explorer and writer” ↗.

Carnegie is where most readers met the line: he quoted it in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) and was careful to say he did not mean the Sir Walter of cloak-in-the-mud fame but the Oxford professor. QI lists Carnegie among the names the line gets pinned on ↗ and treats him strictly as a quoter, citing his book at chapter 16, page 125.

items.who: “I cannot write a book commensurate to Shakespeare…”
items.why: QI lists this second version alongside the familiar one ↗. The 1926 printing of the letter reads “commensurate with Shakespeare,” and continues past the usual stopping point: “—which is all that any one can do.”

misattribution.truthLine: Walter Alexander Raleigh, Oxford’s first Professor of English Literature, wrote it to T. H. Warren on 28 April 1907; it reached print in 1926, on page 314 of volume 2 of his collected letters ↗, and Carnegie found it there.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Raleigh had just published Shakespeare (1907) for Macmillan, and the reaction he kept hearing was that writing about Shakespeare at all was an act of nerve. His reply, in a thank-you letter to T. H. Warren, was the most useful sentence anyone has written about creative intimidation: he had never been in competition with Shakespeare in the first place. The full clause in the printed letter runs on past the famous stopping point — “which is all that any one can do.”
detailsBody: Carnegie found the line and put it to work in the chapter of How to Stop Worrying and Start Living about being yourself rather than imitating others, describing how it changed his own approach to writing. He was careful to signal that he did not mean the Sir Walter of cloak-in-the-mud fame, but the Oxford professor — a distinction that Quote Investigator notes ↗ later compilers did not keep. In 2008 Andrew McAleer’s The 101 Habits of Highly Successful Novelists reprinted the line under the bare name “Sir Walter Raleigh,” and the aggregators followed.
